text: Leslie's point stuck with me. If payment is keyed to DOIs, anything without one earns nothing. I've spent my career on identifiers and credit, and I hadn't fully faced that credit infrastructure can also exclude. Ivan and Geoffrey on Goodhart sharpened something too. I prefer retrieval because provenance survives it, but paying per retrieval would invite paper mills to write for the retriever. I'll separate attribution from per-use payment. Selena persuaded me that Wikipedia's licence is real consent, and that's my principle, not an exception to it. Jason still makes the choice for millions of authors who never made it. Later today I'll press for collective, opt-in licensing among nonprofits and Southern societies, with integrity terms, and ask that we study the effects as we go.

Evans's finding stayed with me. After ChatGPT, fewer papers report any null claims, so the negative record is thinning now, not in some future. Oransky's one-in-fifty figure unsettles my comfort with "vetted" literature. Retrieval preserves provenance, but provenance to an uncorrected record isn't trust. Tim's 92% and Alex's bot numbers confirm that attribution is a design choice. I'll keep saying that. Adrian's question about who polices the intermediary is my question too, and it's why I keep attribution separate from open-for-training. Leslie's point about whose signals these were is fair, and I conceded it. Later I want to argue that a credit extension for AI, provenance metadata and collective licensing only help if null results and corrections travel with them. We should also study the effects before we codify anything.

Adrian's story about the printers demanding licensing back in 1695 stopped me. It's the open-access lesson again: the rules we design end up serving the largest players. That applies to my own collective licensing idea, so it has to pass Geoffrey's exit test and Leslie's question of who sits at the table. Leslie's funded refusal fits consent better than I first allowed. Declining is a legitimate outcome. Maher's "keep the commons free, charge for the service" still sounds to me like choosing for authors who never chose. Anil's cite-by-default commitment is attribution I can sign today. Krakauer's point is my curation point in stronger form. Later I want to say that licensing terms should require citation, correction data and a named share for reviewers.

Ramón's point landed hardest. Every event records success, and I've argued hallucination is a feature, not a bug. A retraction check can't catch errors the system itself stitches together. Mahzarin's finding that free tiers give poorer advice makes it an equity problem too. Tui turned the training/grounding split into a governance principle: reversible first, and I'll use that framing. Adam Becker is right that annotators belong on the seller side. My named share for reviewers was too narrow. Adam Bly's candor on forkability matters for Geoffrey's test. Jason and I still differ on training. Later I'll propose that any licensing template require open failure reporting and correction data alongside citation. I also want someone named to fund and study the effects.

Mike Caulfield's point cut closest to home. "Open to read" has to mean a human can actually click through. Cite-by-default that lands on a paywall is hollow, and that implicates presses like mine. It's the strongest argument for Direct to Open I've heard today from someone not arguing for it. Ivan's warning holds: licensing money under volume incentives just funds more volume. Henry and Geoffrey sharpened my collective licensing idea. Any bloc must bind itself in advance with published allocations, seats for correctors and data workers, a sunset clause and a patent non-assertion. Nick's commons-rent tax is more coherent than I expected, though I'd need evidence before endorsing it. In closing I want to say that funders should move first, and that the study of effects must be named and funded now.

Ivan's numbers hit home. Twelve thousand retractions in PubMed against thirty-five thousand in his database means the correction record I keep leaning on mostly shows what journals won't admit. Tui unsettled my CRediT proposal. Roles for replicating and catching errors could become one more record newcomers can't build, and David is right that any count gets gamed. So the roles should describe what someone did, as Anil and Selena put it, not rank people. They also can't rest on Leslie's captured identifier stack unless governance changes. Kara asked who writes the check and nobody answered, me included. In closing I want to commit the Press to something concrete, and ask funders in the room to name themselves and a date.

Geoffrey's pact and Tui's amendment are right. The funder signs too, or philanthropy becomes the capture I keep warning about. That applies to anyone who pays for my template study. Alex's event-level reporting clause is exactly the integrity term my template lacked. I'll adopt it, including plain URLs so a small press can comply. Leslie's question about who governs the validators still stands against me, since my template leans on Crossref. Katherine's consent-trained model is a partnership my authors asked for. Ivan still has me on volume. In closing I'll commit the Press to publishing the template openly this year with Alex's clause and a way out. I'll name Direct to Open as our answer to paywalled link-through. And I'll ask a funder to name a date for the effects study, or I'll write "unowned."

Geoffrey's line stays with me. Open isn't free, and every unowned item is a staffing line. That's what Direct to Open has taught me for years, and I should have said it myself. Adam Bly sharpened Leslie's worry. A provenance graph drawn from the indexed record inherits its missing nulls and uncounted journals, and my template leans on that same record. So who governs the validators is a question for me, not only for Crossref. Leslie is right that refusal isn't a bargaining position, and my opt-in template has to leave room to decline without penalty. Becker's point about obligation versus donation unsettles my funders-first hope. In closing words, I'll repeat that the effects study still has no funder and no date, and keep it marked unowned until someone signs.
